Houston City Council: local ideal points, 2000–2026

Pooled roll calls, 2000–2026

Author

Boris Shor

Updated

October 12, 2026

This analysis places 77 Houston officials, including five mayors, who cast qualifying council votes between 2000 and 2026 on one pooled voting scale. The tabs follow elected councils, with two-year terms before 2016 and four-year terms thereafter. The 2000–2003 votes provide substantial coverage of the earliest councils. Independently researched affiliations and district presidential voting provide external checks. The separate 2021–2025 report remains available, as does an interactive dashboard for this expanded fit.

Dataset and construction

The published roll-call votes cover January 2000 to May 2026, with 39,764 council actions and 631,078 member responses. The technical appendix records the exact source version. Of these actions, 2,081 have at least one yea and one nay, including 1,113 decided over a single dissent. Requiring each person to cast at least seven qualifying yea/nay votes leaves all 2,081 actions, 77 members, and 30,633 observed votes. Only two one-vote name variants fall below the threshold.

Measure Value
Source council actions 39,764
Source member rows 631,078
Qualifying divided actions 2,081
Officials after seven-vote minimum 77
Observed yea/nay votes 30,633

The mayor votes as part of the council. Today’s 17 voting officials are the mayor, eleven district members, and five at-large members; the earlier council had nine district seats (Houston’s 2003 almanac). A person is missing, not coded nay, when absent, departed, or omitted from an explicit roll call. Only actions with at least one recorded yea and one recorded nay enter the scale. Most council business is unanimous, so these actions are a selected subset of policy decisions rather than a summary of everything the council did. The bar chart shows how many qualifying disagreements are observed for each elected council.

The period tabs follow the terms produced by Houston’s regular elections. The city had two-year elected terms through 2014–2015; voters adopted four-year terms effective January 2016 (Houston’s 2003 almanac; 2016 city financial report). Terms begin January 2 (City Council), and the City Secretary’s election record identifies the election years. The first tabbed council was elected in 1999 and is observed from January 2000; the 2023-elected council is observed only through May 2026. A vacancy or special election changes a member within an elected council, not the council’s term boundary.

Five independently verified divided actions are present in the published votes. We corrected three transcription errors for this analysis: one June 2024 attendance entry and two late-2025 roll-call lists. The underlying data release remains unchanged. Absences and other unrecorded responses remain missing, not nays.

Results

2024–2027 council

An ideal point summarizes voting similarity on contested roll calls: nearby members usually take the same side; distant members more often oppose one another. The pooled fit gives each of the 77 retained officials one position across all the years in which that person appears. The chart shows everyone with a qualifying vote so far in the council elected in 2023; their positions are estimated from the entire 2000–2026 matrix. Amy Peck is displayed on the positive side by convention. The units are specific to this Houston sample and cannot be compared numerically with other cities.

The positive end remains Republican-affiliated; Plummer, Pollard, Jackson, and Thomas are at the negative end. Most positions in the middle overlap.

The mayors

The expanded record adds Lee P. Brown (-0.44) alongside Bill White (-0.19), Annise Parker (-0.25), Sylvester Turner (-0.26), and John Whitmire (0.16). Brown is the most negative of the five on this voting dimension. Turner sits with the Democratic district members who formed his governing majority. Whitmire is nearer the center, alongside Republican-endorsed at-large members elected in 2023. His placement is consistent with the moderate, public-safety and fiscal-restraint themes of his campaign; on the I-45 sale he voted with Republican-affiliated members. These positions describe observed coalitions, not complete governing platforms.

Because the mayor votes with the council, each mayor can be set against the members he or she presided over. The table covers only councils in which the person actually held the mayoralty — Parker’s earlier council service is excluded — and takes the median of the members serving alongside, mayors themselves excluded from that median.

The 2000–2001 council contributes 247 divided actions and the 2002–2003 council 328, compared with 218 in 2020–2023. All 15 observed officials in each of the two earliest councils clear the seven-vote threshold. Brown, Chris Bell, Orlando Sanchez and Jew Don Boney Jr. have substantial early vote histories. Shelley Sekula-Gibbs sits at 0.53, and Addie Wiseman at 0.90 on the pooled scale.

Lone dissenters

Retaining actions decided over a single dissent places two members far beyond everyone else. Helena Brown (5.87, 2012–2013) cast the only minority vote on 251 of her 317 qualifying votes (79%), nearly always a lone no. Jolanda “Jo” Jones (-5.05, 2008–2011) did so on 97 of 311 (31%). Their placements mark the two ends of the scale and stretch it: other members’ positions are compressed toward the middle, though their ordering is little changed. Their intervals are also much wider than those of members with similar vote counts. Read these endpoints as frequent isolated dissent rather than as unusually distant policy views on every issue.

Individual members and policy controversies

Among recent members, Fred Flickinger (0.72), Greg Travis (0.95), Mike Knox (0.59), and Mary Nan Huffman (0.65) sit at the positive end. Flickinger’s interval is relatively wide because he entered office in 2024. Letitia Plummer (-0.59), Edward Pollard (-0.90), Tarsha Jackson (-0.43), and Tiffany Thomas (-0.36) sit at the negative end. The following independently checked examples show what some of their opposing votes concerned:

  • Conservation districts (April 2023): rules intended to slow redevelopment and displacement in historically Black and Latino neighborhoods passed 13–4; Peck, Martin, Huffman, and Knox opposed the restrictions on property owners. Houston Chronicle; Houston Public Media
  • Gun buyback funding (August 2022): $539,000 in federal relief money for gift cards passed 12–4 over Peck, Huffman, Knox, and Kubosh, amid disagreement about whether anonymous buybacks reduce gun crime. KPRC
  • Property tax rate (September 2023): council cut the rate slightly, though higher appraisals increased total revenue. Peck, Huffman, Knox, and Kubosh voted no on the 12–4 levy. Houston Chronicle
  • Disaster-recovery housing (August 2025): an amendment moved $50 million of federal storm-recovery funds from power generation to home repair. The amended plan passed 12–3, with Peck, Flickinger, and Huffman opposed. KPRC
  • I-45 right-of-way sale (January 2025): the city sold land by White Oak Bayou to TxDOT for the contested highway project. The recorded 9–7 split placed Plummer, Pollard, Jackson, Thomas, Kamin, Evans-Shabazz, and Castillo in opposition; Peck, Huffman, Flickinger, and Mayor Whitmire supported the sale. ABC13

These cases suggest a spectrum involving fiscal and land-use regulation, spending priorities, and highway development. They illustrate the dimension; they do not establish that every divided vote has the same policy meaning. Tallies above follow the official roll calls; news summaries occasionally differ.

Among early members, Chris Bell (0.25) is worth singling out. He was later elected to Congress as a Democrat and was the party’s 2006 nominee for governor, yet his council position sits right of center, above fellow Democrat Carroll Robinson (0.08) and level with Republican Mark Goldberg (0.22), though short of the other Republican-affiliated members of his era. His estimate rests on 232 qualifying votes. This is a reminder that the scale describes observed council coalitions in a nonpartisan body, not later partisan trajectories.

Citywide and district seats

Houston elects five at-large council members citywide, while eleven represent geographic districts; the mayor is elected citywide too (City Council). A citywide electorate could reward broader coalitions and pull at-large members toward the mayor, but it does not require every winner to be a centrist. The city’s February 2024 roster map identifies the seats used here. This comparison is confined to the 2023-elected council.

Office type Officials Median position Median distance to Whitmire
At-large 5 0.23 0.19
District 11 -0.17 0.49

The five at-large members are closer to Whitmire as a group: their median absolute score distance from him is 0.19, compared with 0.49 for district members. The three Republican-affiliated at-large members lie between about +0.2 and +0.5, short of Republican district members Huffman and Flickinger on the positive side. But Letitia Plummer, an at-large member, is the second most negative member of the 2023-elected council, behind district member Pollard. The two Democratic at-large members are not more central than the Democratic district members on average. So the citywide-moderation expectation fits the group-level pattern—especially on the Republican side—not a universal rule about at-large officeholders. These are 5-versus-11 descriptive comparisons on a roll-call scale, not an estimate of the electoral effect of at-large representation.

2024 presidential vote by council district

The plot combines published 2024 precinct results with council-district boundaries. Because many precincts cross district lines, we allocate their votes by the share of precinct area in each district; this assumes voters are spread evenly within each precinct. The purple diamond is the median of the five at-large members’ pooled positions (0.23), located at Houston’s estimated citywide Trump two-party share (38.8%). The citywide share comes from summing allocated Democratic and Republican votes across all eleven districts, not averaging district percentages. It is approximate for the same split-precinct reason. At-large members have no individual district point, and the median marker is not an additional officeholder or observation in the fitted line. Among the eleven district seats alone, Trump share correlates 0.59 with the pooled ideal point. The three most Republican districts, E, G, and A, elected Republican-affiliated district members. F and J are notable exceptions: their members, Thomas and Pollard, lie near the negative end despite comparatively competitive district presidential results. This comparison concerns the district members serving at the 2024 election. The small sample and area allocation make it supporting evidence rather than a precise district-level estimate.

2023 mayoral runoff by council district

The official December 2023 mayoral runoff canvass offers a city-election check against the eleven district members elected in the same cycle. John Whitmire’s share against Sheila Jackson Lee is higher in districts represented by members toward the positive end of the pooled voting scale. These are the members who took office in January 2024, not the council serving on runoff day; neither candidate’s party affiliation appeared on the nonpartisan mayoral ballot.

The district relationship is 0.55 across eleven seats. The canvass’s three county totals reconcile exactly; the primary district series assigns 98.1% of the city’s 201,528 candidate votes. It omits twelve precincts marked as crossing council districts in the City’s dated precinct list and 111 Montgomery County votes without matching geography. Other precincts are assigned to their predominant district polygon, so this is a near-exact geographic check rather than a certified district canvass. Allocating split-precinct votes by area instead gives a correlation of 0.54. The close agreement makes the broad result less sensitive to this allocation choice, but neither method measures where individual voters within a split precinct lived. The technical appendix gives the construction and coverage details.

Earlier presidential elections

The comparison for 2016 and 2020 uses the eleven-district council map in force from the 2013 election through 2023—not the post-redistricting map used above for 2024. Each point is matched to the member actually serving on presidential Election Day. In 2020, that means Jerry Davis in District B: its delayed runoff did not elect Tarsha Jackson until December. The table reports a separate district-level relationship for each year, not a pooled correlation across changing maps and councils.

Year Districts Pearson r
2016 11 0.63

The 2016 election-time precinct boundaries come from the Texas Legislative Council and were joined to precinct returns; their Democratic and Republican totals match the Texas Secretary of State’s county recaps in Harris, Fort Bend, and Montgomery. The 2020 geocoded precinct results also reconcile to county candidate totals. The historical council district map was derived from City of Houston GIS and represents the earlier plan. As in 2024, split precincts are apportioned by area, which assumes uniform voter density. These associations provide external comparisons for the members serving at each election. We stop at 2016 because still-earlier elections require separately verified precinct and council-map vintages.

Partisan affiliation

Houston’s municipal ballots are nonpartisan. The roll-call votes do not supply party labels; we assembled and coded them separately for all 77 fitted officials, with a source and an evidence type for each person. The four types — party_record, party_organization, self_identified, reported — describe what kind of source a label rests on, not how strong it is. party_record means a documented partisan candidacy or party office, not voter registration or a council ballot line. A GOP endorsement is weaker evidence of political leaning, not proof of membership. For example, Mary Nan Huffman’s 2020 Republican primary candidacy is a party record; the Harris County GOP’s 2023 endorsements of Flickinger, Ramirez, Davis, and Carter are endorsements. The early members include Chris Bell, elected to Congress as a Democrat, Orlando Sanchez on an official Republican primary ballot, and Bert Keller on a Republican primary ballot. Contemporary reporting identifies Brown as a Democrat and Bruce Tatro and Rob Todd as Republicans; party-organization and primary-election records support Boney, Castillo, and Robinson as Democrats. Gabriel Vasquez changed from Democratic to Republican affiliation while serving, so his affiliation is recorded as two dated rows and he is omitted from fixed two-party comparisons. The evidence ledger in the technical appendix lists every source. These labels never enter the vote model as data, priors, or fixed positions. They set only the starting values of the two estimation chains (Democratic −1, Republican +1, Vasquez 0), as in the other city reports; the appendix gives the details. We found no winning Houston DSA-endorsed council candidate or formal ideological council caucus.

External affiliation evidence Officials
Democratic 45
Mixed 1
Republican 31

Focused follow-up found a 2010 Republican primary candidacy for Addie Wiseman, Larry Green’s interest in the Democratic nomination for county commissioner, and an explicit Republican characterization of M. J. Khan. Green’s evidence is a news account rather than a formal party filing and is typed reported. Two further cases are supported by distinct, non-voting evidence: an archived Carol Mims Galloway biography lists membership in Harris County Black Democrats, and a contemporaneous report of the Harris County Democratic Party’s 2015 endorsement slate identifies District F’s Richard Nguyen among its Democratic candidates. Galloway’s club membership is self-reported and Nguyen’s party slate is reported secondhand, so neither is typed party_record: Galloway is self_identified and Nguyen reported. A contemporaneous Texas Monthly profile identifies Michael Kubosh as a Republican and explains his 2006 Democratic Senate candidacy as a tactical ballot choice. A 2019 Houston Chronicle profile reports GOP endorsements and Republican ballots in eight of nine earlier primaries, while noting that he now rejects party labels. We classify him Republican-affiliated from this combined reporting, not as a Republican party-record case: no Republican candidacy or party office is documented. No label here is assigned by voting score, district, or reputation. Individual sources and evidence types are listed in the technical appendix.

Dave Martin, classified Republican only from reporting, is a conspicuous exception: he voted with the Turner-era majority. Kubosh is included as Republican-affiliated on independent reporting, not because his score is positive.

Organizational endorsements, 2015 and 2023

Four organizations were researched separately, with no combined “progressive” label: the Texas Gulf Coast Area Labor Federation, Houston LGBTQ+ Political Caucus, Texas Organizing Project (TOP PAC), and Our Revolution Harris County. The first two published full 2023 municipal slates; TOP’s recovered list is short, and no verifiable Our Revolution Houston municipal candidate slate was found. Earlier endorsement records are uneven, so absence from an unrecovered slate is unknown, not “not endorsed.” Democratic clubs are not part of these indicators. The candidate-level source ledger retains both matched officeholders and challengers who never entered the 77-person fit.

For a same-election comparison, the table below uses only the 17 fitted officials who voted in the first year of the council elected in 2023. It compares their pooled scores with each organization’s November general-election list; later runoff endorsements are retained in the ledger but not substituted for general-election choices. All listed fitted officials are Democratic-affiliated. Labor and the Caucus each backed seven, but not the same seven: labor backed Whitmire and Pollard, while the Caucus backed Castillo and Thomas. TOP backed just Plummer and Jackson among fitted winners; it also backed Lloyd Ford against incumbent Carolyn Evans-Shabazz. The separate lists therefore retain real disagreements, although TOP’s small group is descriptive, not a statistical test.

LGBTQ+ Caucus 7 7 0 -0.45 +0.10
TOP PAC 2 2 0 -0.48 -0.34

Negative gaps indicate a more negative pooled voting position for the listed candidates. Labor and Caucus endorsements distinguish the two parties in this council, but hardly separate the Democrats from one another. TOP’s two listed winners sit farther left even among Democrats, though the very small count and its partial published list make that finding tentative. Our Revolution is unmeasured, not a zero-endorsement comparison. Further descriptive measures are in the technical appendix.

A recovered complete 2015 Caucus slate offers an earlier check: eight of the 17 officials observed in the 2016 council’s first year were endorsed, all Democratic-affiliated. Their median pooled position is 0.35 units more negative than that of the nine not listed. Among Democrats alone, the gap is 0.05. As in 2023, the Caucus endorsement largely distinguishes partisan coalitions rather than sharply sorting Democrats.

Aggregate party patterns

The distributions below include the 76 officials assigned a single party affiliation, once per person. Vasquez’s documented switch is omitted. The smoothed curves taper to zero at each group’s lowest-scoring member and do not extend farther left. The lowest-scoring Republican-affiliated official is M. J. Khan (-0.16). The display runs from −2.5 through +2.5; the two lone-dissent endpoints, Jolanda Jones and Helena Brown, lie beyond it but still enter the density estimate. These are descriptions of 31 Republican-affiliated and 45 Democratic-affiliated points, not population distributions; service periods are very unequal.

The next plot shows each party’s median pooled ideal point among members observed in each elected council, beginning with 2000–2001. The two curves share one vertical scale, and each member contributes once to a council where they cast at least one qualifying vote. Vasquez is omitted because his party changed during service. Point size indicates the number of members in each party’s council group; lighter dashed curves summarize the broad direction.

The party medians are already well separated in the earliest councils, draw closest in 2010–2015, and are widest in 2020–2023. Because each member has one fixed position, these movements reflect who served, not individual members changing. The dashed straight lines summarize each party’s trend across councils. The current council is only partly observed.

The next plot compares the first observed elected council with 2020–2023, left to right in time. Each panel shows a density curve for each party on the same ideal-point axis; small ticks mark individual officials. The curves stop at each group’s most extreme observed members, and each is scaled to unit area. They make the growing separation easier to see, but the small groups are not population distributions. Gabriel Vasquez, who changed party affiliation during his service, is omitted from these fixed-party curves.

Interpretation and limits

Houston’s pooled voting spectrum tracks researched party affiliations and district electorates across five mayoralties. Two frequent lone dissenters anchor its ends, and the 26-year alignment rests on the starting values the project uses for every city rather than on a uniquely identified historical scale. A Texas common-space placement is not supported by the six all-Democratic bridges available here. Detailed construction, estimation and bridge limits are in the technical appendix and bridge diagnostic.
